title: Divisibility Rules OQ-01-OQ-02: A Power-of-10 Digit-Sum Base Exists for Every Modulus Coprime to 10
description: Resolves the parent's open question: for EVERY modulus d coprime to 10 there is a power-of-10 base B = 10^k (with k > 0) for which the digit-sum divisibility rule holds, d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (digits (10^k) n).sum for all n. The witness is k = φ(d) via the Fermat–Euler theorem. A sharp characterization shows the valid exponents are exactly the multiples of the multiplicative order ord_d(10) = orderOf (10 : ZMod d), so 10^{ord_d(10)} is the smallest power-of-10 base that works. The single existence theorem subsumes every digit-sum instance in the parent and yields new ones (genuine base-10^6 digit-sum rules for 7 and 13, which the parent obtained only by truncation). Fully machine-checked with no axioms beyond Lean's foundational triple and no sorries; all base-side conditions are discharged by kernel `decide` (not native_decide), so the file is free of Lean.ofReduceBool.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None beyond Lean/Mathlib's foundational axioms. Every headline theorem (exists_pow_ten_digitSum_rule, digitSum_rule_pow_totient, pow_modEq_one_iff_order_dvd, orderOf_least_valid_exponent, minimal_pow_ten_digitSum_rule) and the concrete instances depend only on [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound], verified by #print axioms. The base-side congruences are discharged by kernel `decide` over decidable ℕ-arithmetic (not native_decide), so the proof does NOT depend on Lean.ofReduceBool.
originalContributions: Universal existence theorem: for every d ≥ 2 coprime to 10 a positive exponent k makes 10^k a valid digit-sum base (exists_pow_ten_digitSum_rule), with explicit witness k = φ(d)
Sharp characterization via the multiplicative order: 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) ↔ orderOf (10 : ZMod d) ∣ k (pow_modEq_one_iff_order_dvd)
Minimality: ord_d(10) is the least positive valid exponent (orderOf_least_valid_exponent), so 10^{ord_d(10)} is the smallest working power-of-10 base
New concrete digit-sum rules in base 10^6 for 7 and 13 (parent reached these only via truncation)
0-axiom, native_decide-free formalization (cleaner than the parent, which depends on Lean.ofReduceBool)

overview.historicalContext: The casting-out-nines and digit-sum rules rest on the congruence 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3) and (mod 9), and the grouping rules for 37, 27, 99, 101, 999 rest on 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) for suitable k. The parent gallery entry collected such rules for a hand-picked list of moduli, each paired with an ad hoc base. The natural completion — which moduli admit a power-of-10 digit-sum base at all? — is answered by elementary group theory: 10 is invertible modulo d exactly when gcd(10, d) = 1, and then its multiplicative order ord_d(10) is finite (Lagrange / Fermat–Euler). Any multiple of that order gives 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d), so the digit-sum rule applies; the order itself gives the smallest base. This is the standard explanation for why 7 and 13 have base-10^6 digit-sum rules (ord_7(10) = ord_13(10) = 6) and why 3 needs only base 10 (ord_3(10) = 1).
overview.problemStatement: Prove that for every modulus d coprime to 10 there exists a base B that is a power of 10 such that d ∣ n if and only if d divides the sum of the base-B digits of n (the parent's second open question, which phrases it as the digit-sum OR alternating-digit-sum rule; the digit-sum branch settles the disjunction in full). Additionally, characterize exactly which power-of-10 bases work and identify the minimal one.
overview.proofStrategy: The workhorse lemma digitSum_rule_of_modEq_one reduces the digit-sum rule for base 10^k to the single congruence 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d), wrapping Mathlib's Nat.modEq_digits_sum into an iff via Nat.ModEq.dvd_iff. Existence (exists_pow_ten_digitSum_rule) then supplies k = φ(d) through the Fermat–Euler theorem Nat.ModEq.pow_totient, with positivity from Nat.totient_pos. The sharp characterization pow_modEq_one_iff_order_dvd transports the congruence into ZMod d (via ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff) and applies orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one, identifying the valid exponents as the multiples of orderOf (10 : ZMod d). Positivity of the order (orderOf_ten_pos) is forced because the order divides φ(d) > 0, and minimality (orderOf_least_valid_exponent) is Nat.le_of_dvd. Concrete instances follow by discharging 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) with kernel decide.
keyInsights: A digit-sum divisibility rule in base B = 10^k holds for d precisely because B ≡ 1 (mod d); the whole theory collapses to controlling the single congruence 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d).
Coprimality of 10 and d is exactly the condition under which 10 is a unit in ZMod d, hence has finite multiplicative order — this is what makes a power-of-10 base exist at all.
The set of valid exponents is the subgroup of multiples of ord_d(10): every working base is a power of the minimal base 10^{ord_d(10)}, and no smaller positive power of 10 works.
Euler's theorem gives the non-sharp witness k = φ(d) for free; sharpness requires passing to the order, which divides φ(d) (Lagrange).
Because the order divides the positive number φ(d), it cannot be 0, so for coprime d the minimal base 10^{ord_d(10)} is genuinely non-degenerate (≠ 1).
Using kernel `decide` rather than `native_decide` for the finite congruence checks keeps the entry free of Lean.ofReduceBool, so it is genuinely 0-axiom — a strict improvement over the parent.
prerequisites: The Fermat–Euler theorem (Nat.ModEq.pow_totient) and Euler's totient (Nat.totient_pos)
Multiplicative order in a monoid (orderOf, orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one) and ZMod d casts

conclusion.summary: Twelve theorems establish that a power-of-10 digit-sum base exists for every modulus coprime to 10, identify the valid exponents as the multiples of the multiplicative order of 10, and pin the minimal working base at 10^{ord_d(10)}. Five concrete instances (3, 7, 13, 27, 37) are recovered as corollaries, including new base-10^6 rules for 7 and 13.
conclusion.implications: This upgrades the parent's list of individually proved rules to a universal existence-and-sharpness statement: the question 'which moduli have a power-of-10 digit-sum rule?' is answered completely (all d coprime to 10) and the optimal base is characterized. The 0-axiom, native_decide-free proof also tightens the parent's Lean.ofReduceBool dependency.
openQuestions: Characterize exactly which d coprime to 10 admit an alternating-digit-sum rule (i.e. when -1 is a power of 10 mod d), equivalently when ord_d(10) is even and 10^{ord_d(10)/2} ≡ -1 (mod d).
Give the analogous existence/minimality theory for an arbitrary radix r in place of 10: a digit-sum base r^k exists for d iff gcd(r, d) = 1, with minimal exponent ord_d(r).

sections.title: Header: Universal Power-of-10 Bases for Digit-Sum Rules
sections.summary: Module docstring: notes the parent file only proved digit-sum divisibility rules for a hand-picked list of moduli, states the open question's universal claim — every modulus d coprime to 10 admits a power-of-10 base 10^k with d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ digitsum, witnessed by k=φ(d) via Fermat–Euler — and that the exact valid exponents are the multiples of the multiplicative order ord_d(10).
sections.mathContext: For every $d$ coprime to 10, $d \mid n \iff d \mid \sum \mathrm{digits}(10^k, n)$ for $k=\varphi(d)$ (Fermat–Euler: $10^{\varphi(d)}\equiv 1 \pmod d$), and more sharply for every multiple of $\mathrm{ord}_d(10) = \mathrm{orderOf}(10 : \mathbb Z/d)$, the minimal such exponent.

sections.title: Part I: The General Digit-Sum Rule from 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d)
sections.summary: digitSum_rule_of_modEq_one reduces a base-10^k digit-sum rule for d ≥ 2 to the single congruence 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d), via Nat.modEq_digits_sum and Nat.ModEq.dvd_iff. exists_pow_ten_digitSum_rule then proves the universal existence statement with witness k = φ(d) (Fermat–Euler), and digitSum_rule_pow_totient records the explicit base 10^{φ(d)}.

sections.title: Part II: Sharp Characterization via the Multiplicative Order
sections.summary: pow_modEq_one_iff_order_dvd characterizes the valid exponents as the multiples of orderOf (10 : ZMod d) by transporting the congruence into ZMod d and applying orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one. orderOf_ten_pos shows the order is positive (it divides φ(d) > 0), orderOf_least_valid_exponent establishes minimality, and minimal_pow_ten_digitSum_rule packages the smallest working base 10^{ord_d(10)}.

sections.title: Part III: Concrete Instances
sections.summary: Corollaries of digitSum_rule_of_modEq_one: divisibility by 3 (base 10), 7 and 13 (base 10^6, new), 27 and 37 (base 10^3). Each discharges its congruence 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) by kernel decide.

sections.title: Part IV: Numerical Sanity Checks
sections.summary: Decidable checks of the driving modular facts: ord_7(10) ∣ 6 and ord_13(10) ∣ 6 (so 10^6 is valid), 10^3 ≢ 1 (mod 7) (a smaller base fails for 7), and 10^6 ≡ 1 (mod 13). #check commands expose the headline theorem names.
